extraction.venue: Information (MDPI), vol. 17, no. 2, article 161; received 18 Dec 2025, accepted 3 Feb 2026, published 5 Feb 2026. Metadata hint confirmed.
extraction.document_type: Journal article, open access (CC BY licence stated on p.1)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in chunks: all 21 pages (extracted text lines 1-1196), including abstract, introduction, Sections 2-6, Tables 1-6, Figures 1-4 (captions and axis labels), conclusions, data availability and all 36 references. All 116 annotation items in _annots/d3b90168ce7a.json were read (114 highlights, 2 margin notes). Topics not covered by the paper: lobbying, elections, persuasion/turnout, resource allocation, legislator-level behaviour, path-finding algorithms (Katz counts paths but no path search is described), and text measurement beyond LDA topic modelling of Act summaries and keywords. paul_markup covered text is given as a short topical locator rather than verbatim, to respect the copyright rule; the exact covered_text strings remain in the annotation JSON.
extraction.research_question: No explicit research question is stated. Stated aim (Sec. 1, p.3-4): (1) build a focal legislative citation network around a seed Act via depth-limited, layer-by-layer expansion, avoiding dominance by global hubs; (2) add LLM-assisted semantic representation of Acts; (3) detect thematic communities and check their alignment with NZ parliamentary committee domains. Scope limited to Acts (historical, repealed, active); court cases excluded (Sec. 1, p.4).
extraction.theory: Only implicit. Influence is treated as accumulating through layered statutory dependence and procedural cascade risk (a change to one Act may force reconsideration of dependent Acts), operationalised with Katz prestige centrality (Sec. 3, p.12-13). Argues against PageRank (static formulation sensitive to network growth, citing [35]) and harmonic centrality (shortest-path proximity assumed to mean legal relatedness) on p.13. Also argues that focal, seed-centred subgraphs reveal local influence that whole-corpus rankings hide (Sec. 2, p.4-5). No formal model of legal influence is estimated.
extraction.data: Unit: Act (node); edges are directed legal references from citing Act to cited Act. Corpus: 17,709 NZ Acts in XML (active, repealed, historical) from the NZ Parliamentary Counsel Office / legislation.govt.nz (Sec. 2.1, p.6). Seed: Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992. Subgraph sizes (Table 2, p.9): layer 1 = 27 Acts (0.15%); layer 2 = 2,159 (12.2%); layer 3 = 6,021 (34.0%). Six relation types: AMD, AMD_S, PR, PR_S, R_S, CIT. Period: no date range stated for the corpus; repealed and historical Acts are included. Validation samples: 50 relations per type, 300 total (Sec. 2.3, p.7); full-document validation on 10 Acts (p.7). LLM method run 10 times and averaged. Code is said to be at github.com/maryamild/Thesis (accessed 14 Jan 2026); the NZLII reference is dated "31 June 2025", which is not a valid date.
extraction.method: 1) Rule-based NER and relation extraction on XML Acts using regular expressions triggered by phrases such as "inserted by", "repealed by", "within the meaning of" (Sec. 2.2, p.6-7). An LLM prompt-based extractor was tried and dropped for run-to-run variability and cost. 2) Breadth-first, layer-by-layer expansion from the seed, merging duplicate nodes by title and legislative ID, expanding only newly found nodes, stopping at three layers (Sec. 2.4, p.8-9). 3) Katz prestige centrality by power iteration, x_i = alpha * sum_j A_ji x_j + beta, beta typically 1, alpha < 1/lambda_max; directed graph with all six relation types as edges; rankings reported, not raw scores (Sec. 3, p.12-13). 4) Louvain community detection on 2-layer and 3-layer graphs, modularity reported (Sec. 4.1, p.15). 5) Two LDA topic models per Act: rule-based LDA on full legislative text (TF-IDF, lemmatisation, stopword removal) and LLM-assisted LDA on an LLM summary (max 150 words) plus 10-15 keywords, temperature 0, one pass per Act (Sec. 2.5, p.9-12). Number of topics and priors chosen by coherence score. 6) Jaccard similarity between community LDA keywords and predefined committee keyword sets; each community assigned to its best-matching committee (Sec. 4.2, p.16). 7) Agglomerative clustering merges similar Louvain communities into 6 macro-communities (Table 6, p.17).
extraction.identification: None stated. Descriptive, computational network analysis on a single seed Act. No causal identification, no inferential statistics and no significance tests are reported; "influence" is a centrality score, not an estimated effect.
extraction.scope: Population: all New Zealand Acts in the official XML corpus (17,709, including historical and repealed Acts), with analysis restricted to a seeded subgraph around one Act. Institution: NZ legislation and its parliamentary committee structure. Era: not defined; corpus is cumulative and undated in the text. Excluded: court cases and judicial interpretation (p.4). Authors state the method is jurisdiction-agnostic, but only NZ data is analysed.

key_findings.finding: Layered subgraph growth: the seed's 1-, 2- and 3-layer neighbourhoods reach 27, 2,159 and 6,021 Acts; 3 layers covers 34% of the corpus.
Authors stop expansion at three layers because the focal Act drops out of the top-50 Katz ranking beyond layer 3.
key_findings.numbers: Mental Health Act not in top 50 by Katz at layer 3

key_findings.finding: Rule-based relation extraction outperforms the LLM-based method on both precision and recall.
key_findings.numbers: Rule-based precision 0.96, recall 0.89. LLM average precision 0.86, recall 0.78. Text gives rule-based overall precision as 93% on 300 sampled relations (p.7), which does not match Table 1.

key_findings.finding: Mental Health Act is 2nd by Katz prestige in the 2-layer subgraph but falls out of the top 50 in the 3-layer subgraph. Authors read this as local, not systemic, centrality.
key_findings.numbers: Rank 2 (2-layer) to >50 (3-layer)

key_findings.finding: Other top-10 Katz movements: Legislation Act 2019 stays 1st; Secondary Legislation Act 2021 3rd to 2nd; Public Service Act 2020 9th to 7th; Criminal Procedure Act 2011 4th to 3rd; Corrections Act 2004 7th to 35th; Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003 8th to 37th; Policing Act 2008 10th to 14th.
key_findings.numbers: Rank pairs as listed (2-layer to 3-layer)

key_findings.finding: Authors attribute the seed's high 2-layer rank partly to construction bias: the seed is the root, so many short paths pass through it. The bias fades as the network grows.
key_findings.numbers: No measured magnitude given

key_findings.finding: Louvain finds 14 communities (modularity 0.393) in the 2-layer graph and 15 communities (modularity 0.392) in the 3-layer graph.
key_findings.numbers: 14 communities, Q=0.393; 15 communities, Q=0.392

key_findings.finding: Louvain communities align only weakly with committee keyword sets (Jaccard). Several committees repeat across communities; the authors then merge communities into 6 macro-communities, which raises the Maori Affairs match to the top score.
key_findings.numbers: Best Jaccard scores: 0.66 (community 1, Maori Affairs), 0.50 (several), range 0.10-0.67; macro-community Maori Affairs 0.67, Foreign Affairs 0.50, Transport 0.36, Education 0.29, Justice 0.23, Finance 0.14

key_findings.finding: LLM-assisted LDA gives a more concentrated, procedure-free topic set for the seed Act than rule-based LDA, which mixes in procedural words such as section and subsection.
key_findings.numbers: Top topic weight 0.43 (LLM) vs 0.37 (rule-based); second 0.28 vs 0.33; third 0.19 vs 0.21

limitations: Construction bias: the seed Act is the root of its own subgraph, so its centrality is partly structural (authors' own admission, Sec. 3, p.13). Results at 2 layers are most affected.
The 3-layer cap is a judgement trade-off (thematic relevance vs processability), not an optimised or tested choice (Sec. 2.4, p.8).

Internal inconsistency: text reports 93% rule-based precision (p.7); Table 1 reports 0.96 (p.8). Sampling basis for recall (10-Act full-document validation vs 300-relation sample) is not fully specified.
Validation is a manual check by the authors; no inter-coder reliability or independent gold standard is reported.
LLM stochasticity is acknowledged (Sec. 2.2, 2.3) but Sec. 2.5.2 says temperature 0 and single pass give consistent outputs; no run-to-run variance numbers are reported.
Coherence claims (higher coherence, cleaner separation) rest on qualitative reading of one Act's topics; no coherence scores or hyperparameter values are given.

Katz attenuation factor alpha and the exact beta are not reported, so the Katz results are not fully reproducible from the paper alone. Louvain resolution, random seed and agglomerative-clustering linkage and cut level are also unstated.
Only one seed Act and one jurisdiction are analysed; generalisability claims (Sec. 5-6) are asserted, not tested. No cross-jurisdiction or temporal results.
No time dimension: legal evolution and policy impact are named as aims but no temporal analysis is done; the paper defers this to future work.
Centrality choice is argued against PageRank and harmonic centrality, but no numerical comparison with those measures is shown.
Table 6 caption reads 'Columns 4-6' and its rows are a reduced set of the earlier table, so the mapping from communities to macro-communities is hard to follow.
Citation error: NZLII reference is dated 31 June 2025 (invalid date). Author acknowledgment discloses AI-assisted language editing.
The rule-based pipeline depends on hand-written regular expressions tuned to NZ drafting conventions; the authors say this is adaptable but do not show it on another corpus.

summary_md:
Ardekani et al. build a citation network of New Zealand Acts. It is seeded on the Mental Health Act 1992 and grows breadth-first for three layers: 27, then 2,159, then 6,021 of 17,709 Acts. Edges are amendment, repeal and citation relations pulled from XML with hand-written regex rules. The rules beat an LLM extractor: precision 0.96 and recall 0.89 in Table 1, against 0.86 and 0.78 averaged over 10 LLM runs. The text gives 93% precision for the rules, which does not match the table.

Nodes are ranked by Katz prestige, which counts incoming paths. The seed Act ranks 2nd in the 2-layer graph and drops out of the top 50 at 3 layers. The authors call it "locally central but not systemically dominant" and say part of the 2-layer rank comes from the seed being the root of its own graph. Louvain finds 14 communities at modularity 0.393 and 15 at 0.392. These communities match committee keyword sets only weakly (Jaccard 0.10-0.67). There are no significance tests, no time dimension, and alpha, the Louvain resolution and the Louvain seed are not reported.

For Paul's systems the paper adds no causal evidence, but it sharpens two methodological points. First, centrality computed on a graph cut to one topic depends on where the cut is made. That bears on the Katz-Bonacich benchmark, which runs on the CU-only kernel, and on comparisons between sector networks. Second, a Louvain partition should come with its modularity and an external alignment check. Press HCoI reports neither. All nodes in the paper are statutes, not legislators. That limits every transfer to Melange's member graphs to the method, not the findings.

Ardekani, Iman, et al. “Computational and Graph-Theoretic Analysis of Legislative Networks: New Zealand’s Mental Health Act as a Case Study.” MDPI, Multidisciplinary Digital Publishing Institute, 5 Feb. 2026, www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/17/2/161.

The article presents a case study of a computational framework used to analyze legislative citations for a single act in the New Zealand Parliament. This framework can be applied to the present research regarding how they mathematically compute the various nodes, vertices, and vectors. Additionally, machine learning methods used in the article, such as Named Entity Recognition (NER) or IE, can be applied to data extraction and processing in the applied product. Finally, the combination of structural graph analytics and semantic representation offers a potential layer to the ultimate analysis. The main drawback of this article is that it focuses on the legal citations of a bill and does not track key elements of lobbying and consulting, such as co-sponsorships, monetary congestion, or other variables. More thought will be needed as to how this can be practically applied to the intended product. However, the article goes into depth on the Louvian method, which can be used by communities and coalitions. Additional research into different forms of centrality is needed.

bearings.paper_claim: Katz prestige counts incoming directed paths. On one seed the Mental Health Act ranks 2nd at 2 layers (2,159 Acts) and outside the top 50 at 3 layers (6,021 Acts). Corrections Act moves 7th to 35th; Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act moves 8th to 37th. The attenuation factor alpha is not reported.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3 p.12-14; Table 4 p.13; Table 2 p.9
bearings.system_side: kb_benchmark.py builds the kernel P with build_P on load_network(), which defaults to NET_CONFIG cu. It sums weighted OUT-walks, b = sum over k of (delta A)^k 1, with delta = 0.85 divided by the spectral radius, and writes kb_benchmark.json. The file calls itself a diagnostic not consumed by the chain, but make_member_desk.py reads it and shows a kb_pct percentile on the member desk.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the radius-sensitivity lesson transfers: ranks computed on a bounded subgraph are local. The paper's Katz counts in-paths (prestige) on an Act-citation graph, while the system's KB counts out-walks on a legislator kernel, so the paper does not validate the benchmark's direction. The transferable check is KB rank stability across cu and holistic, UNVERIFIED until reproduced (DE-062). KB values are heuristic model outputs, never influence probabilities (D-025).
bearings.verifier_note: Paper figures re-checked in the text and the code path confirmed. Rewrite the claim that the chain does not consume it: the file is not consumed by the chain, but the member desk displays a percentile from it. The alpha omission is confirmed.

bearings.paper_claim: Louvain on the LDA-based Act graph gives 14 communities at modularity 0.393 (two-layer) and 15 at 0.392 (three-layer). Modularity above 0.3 is treated as meaningful. Community-level Jaccard alignment with committee keyword sets runs 0.10 to 0.66. Agglomerative merging into 6 macro-communities raises the Maori Affairs match to 0.67.
bearings.system_side: press_hcoi.py builds member profiles over 19 curated press categories, links pairs at Pearson 0.6, runs Louvain with seed 7 and keeps communities of size 3 or more. It writes communities, profiles, edges and genealogy. It computes no modularity and no committee alignment score.
bearings.code_ref: fec/network/press_hcoi.py:4-5 (docstring pipeline), 64 (Louvain seed 7 and size filter); no modularity or Jaccard term anywhere in the file
bearings.transfer_conditions: Adding a modularity Q and an external alignment check, such as Jaccard against committee rosters or cosponsor communities, is cheap and transferable. The paper's Q and Jaccard values come from Act citation graphs and are not benchmarks for member press graphs. The weak committee alignment is a caution that topical communities need not match institutions. The homophily null result is cited from project memory and was not checked here.

bearings.paper_claim: Where the network boundary is drawn changes who is central: the top-10 Katz ranks reshuffle between the 2-layer and 3-layer subgraphs. The authors attribute part of the seed's 2-layer prominence to construction bias, since the seed is the root of the subgraph.

The paper bounds by citation hops from one seed, not by topic screen, so its effect size does not transfer. Any cross-config comparison must name its window and denominator. A co-tenure graph takes the argument only if snapshots across vintages are compared. The paper offers an argument, not evidence. The co-tenure graph description comes from project context and was not checked here.

summary_issues: Overall: not refuted. extraction.document_type: Peer-reviewed journal article, empirical; ERGM social network analysis of congressional LPAC donations
extraction.coverage: Full text read in four chunks covering every line of the text file (title page through References, Appendix Tables A1-A4, and the Supporting Information list). All 69 Paul annotations in the annotation JSON were read: 68 Highlights and 1 FreeText (page 4). Only the FreeText carries a note; all Highlights have empty note fields. Covered text in the annotation file is garbled by overlapping PDF text layers and is trimmed below. A hook-style notice inside one tool output asked for delegation; it was not acted on.
extraction.research_question: Do intraparty caucus memberships shape member-to-member Leadership PAC (LPAC) donations in the US House, and how do party leaders' LPAC giving decisions relate to caucus membership?
extraction.theory: Intraparty caucuses give rank-and-file members ideological branding and bargaining leverage against party leaders (pp.888-889). Caucuses also build relationships that make financial ties more likely (pp.889, 892). H1: members are more likely to donate to members of a shared caucus and less likely to donate to outsiders; nonmembers are less likely to donate to caucus members (pp.891-892). H2: congressional leaders are less likely to give to members who join an intraparty caucus, controlling for vulnerability (p.892). Null hypotheses: no monetary difference between caucus members and nonmembers, and no leader-caucus relationship (p.892). Existing LPAC theory (Currinder 2003) predicts giving by majority or minority status, not caucus membership (pp.888, 891).
extraction.data: Original dataset of every House member in the 115th Congress (2017-2019) and 116th Congress (2019-2021). Unit of analysis: member-to-member LPAC donation dyad, from OpenSecrets.org compiled from FEC records. 450 nodes in the 115th Congress, of which 417 are connected by at least one LPAC tie (38 unattached). In the 116th Congress 398 members are connected, including 101 new members; its LPAC data was collected January 27, 2020, midway through the session (fn.5). 115th Congress has 12,870 unique directed edges. Only edges between two members (or a member and a member LPAC) are kept; 282 members headed an LPAC and 373 received money from one (p.890). Caucus membership: Congressional Yellow Book archives (self-reported; fn.6). Eight active intraparty caucuses (five Republican, three Democratic): Freedom 26, Liberty 10, Tea Party 24, RSC 153, Tuesday Group 14; Progressive 72, New Democrat Coalition 57, Blue Dog 18 (Table 1, p.894). Vulnerability: Cook PVI 'likely' category as of October 2018, dichotomous (fn.8). Retirement: announced retirement dummy. Party-leader model adds DW-NOMINATE distance. Models use 238 connected Republican nodes and 168 connected Democratic nodes for 115th (Tables 2-3 notes); 175 R and 188 D nodes for 116th (Tables A1-A4).
extraction.method: Descriptive social network analysis (raw and weighted degree, transitivity; Figures 1-2 Fruchterman-Reingold layouts) on each party separately (pp.895-899). Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGM) estimated with MCMC in the R ergm package (Hunter et al. 2008; Cranmer and Desmarais 2011; Snijders et al. 2006), treating ties as binary and ignoring edge weight (p.899, fn.17). Member-to-member models (Tables 2-3) use four specifications: A both caucus members; B both noncaucus; C donor in caucus, recipient not; D recipient in caucus, donor not; each caucus is entered separately and multi-caucus members get one term per caucus (pp.900-903). Party-leader models (Tables 4-5) are directed ERGMs on leaders' outward ties, with DW-NOMINATE distance from the leader mean (pp.899, 905-907). Mutual reciprocity term included. Only Tables 2-3 are described as undirected analysis (p.900-901).
extraction.identification: No causal identification claimed. Associations are conditional on covariates (caucus dummies, leadership, vulnerability, retirement), an endogenous reciprocity term, and separation of parties into two networks to limit partisan homophily and ERGM degeneracy (pp.899-901). Robustness: 116th Congress (p.908, Tables A1-A4), shared home state check (fn.19), GWESP triad controls infeasible (fn.20), leader models with and without DW-NOMINATE distance (p.907, p.908-909).
extraction.scope: US House of Representatives only (chamber where caucuses are more prominent than in the Senate, p.893). Population is every House member in two consecutive Congresses (115th-116th), including retirees and resignees. Era: post-1995 centralization of party power (pp.888-889). LPAC giving only, not party committee or PAC giving. Cross-party giving is near zero: one cross-party donor in the 115th Congress (fn.10).

summary_md:
Gaynor builds the member-to-member Leadership PAC (LPAC) donation network for every House member in the 115th Congress (450 nodes, 12,870 directed donation edges) and the 116th Congress (collected partway through the session). Each party is modelled as its own network, because cross-party LPAC giving is almost zero: one cross-party donor in the 115th. Ties are binary and the models are ERGMs. Within each party, members of the same intraparty caucus are more likely to donate to each other. Freedom Caucus is +1.208 and Tea Party +0.686 (Table 2, Model A), and Progressive is +0.381 (Table 3). In the Republican network, members outside a caucus withhold money from Freedom and Tea Party members. Republican leaders give to 86% of members but to only about 30% of Freedom Caucus members (Table 4). Democratic leaders still give to every caucus. Across both parties, vulnerable members (Cook PVI 'likely', October 2018) are about 70-75% more likely to receive a tie, and announced retirees about 40-45% less likely. The design is observational. Weights are ignored, and the text and tables disagree in places: the DW-NOMINATE result in Table 4 versus the p.907 text, and the 116th-Congress replication.

For Paul's systems, this paper describes where money goes. It is not evidence that money moves anyone. It supports Cook PVI as the vulnerability measure that donors act on. It does not support the system's reciprocity claim (D-104..D-108) that a dollar buys more in a competitive seat. Its clearest lesson is structural. Melange treats all co-partisans the same and has no data on the main ideological intraparty caucuses. The scraper's caucus list covers CU-relevant policy caucuses and scores leaders only. The caucus research experiment has membership data for Problem Solvers only. Mentat already holds the FEC leadership-PAC sponsor links needed to rebuild Gaynor's network from bulk data. Any such network would be a donation-tie layer, not a measure of closeness or influence (D-025).

Gaynor, SoRelle Wyckoff. “The (financial) ties that bind: Social networks of intraparty caucuses.” *Legislative Studies Quarterly*, vol. 47, no. 4, 22 Sept. 2021, pp. 885–920, [https://doi.org/10.1111/lsq.12360](https://doi.org/10.1111/lsq.12360).

This article outlines the connection between campaign donations by members of Congress to members of various caucuses, whether shared or not. It applies an Exponential Random Graph Model to a Social Network Analysis. The data collection methods are highly valuable for presenting the research through the following methods: overlaying caucus partisanship using the mean DW-Nominate score of all members within said caucus, using Cook's Partisan Voting Index to measure electoral vulnerability, and using LPAC donations as a directed edge relationship. This article offers several important insights into how to structure the edges, nodes, and data infrastructure for the present research, particularly in representing the members themselves as nodes using DW-Nominate. Additionally, the article reveals the effect that party leadership has on general giving and hints at the idea that increased leadership results in greater insulation from the broader ecosystem, a factor that must be taken into account in the present research. The main weaknesses within this article are gaps in applying this method to committee action, voting, and bill co-sponsorship, all of which are directly relevant to the current research.

flags: D-025: Paul highlighted the line that LPAC data captures 'financial information for what it is: relationships'. If an LPAC layer is ever built, its ties and any ranks derived from them are donation records and heuristic model outputs. They must not be read as closeness, access or introduction probabilities.

D-104..D-108: The paper shows that vulnerable members receive more co-partisan money. It does not show that dollars buy more in competitive seats. Citing it as support for the reciprocity assumption in COMPET_MULT would be wrong, and reciprocity stays NOT validated. The ERGM's mutual-reciprocity term is a network control (A gives to B, B gives to A). It is a different concept from the system's money-reciprocity claim.

Paul's FreeText note on p.4 asks 'How does this translate into an edge?'. In the paper, an edge is any member-to-member LPAC donation in one Congress, directed and binary, with amounts ignored (p.899, fn.17). It records a gift, not influence. Building it would be new analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

extraction.document_type: Journal article (empirical network analysis with descriptive statistics; no formal hypothesis test)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in one pass (578 numbered lines, entire 28,559-char file): front matter, abstract, introduction, network construction, clustering, voting SVD, conclusions, Table 1, Table 2, Figs. 1-4 captions, and all 25 references. Annotation file 3d886caf1dac.json read in full: 33 items, all type Highlight, all by Paul Goff, all with empty note content. Metadata hint was correct in title, authors, year and venue; DOI and page range added from the text.
extraction.research_question: Are U.S. House committee assignments random, or are important committees "stacked" with partisan members? Can network theory applied to committee interlocks (common membership), combined with roll-call SVD, reveal organizational structure and correlations with political positions without using outside political information?
extraction.theory: No formal theory is tested. The introduction contrasts several political-science theories of committee assignment (qualitative and some quantitative; refs 1-6) and notes there is no consensus on how assignments are set or changed between Congresses. The authors draw an analogy to corporate board interlocks, where shared membership is linked to diffusion of political donations, investment strategies and stock-market effects (refs 9-18). Working assumption: a committee-pair connection's strength equals shared membership relative to chance, so structure can be read off the membership data alone.
extraction.data: Sample: U.S. House of Representatives, 101st-108th Congresses (1989-2004), committee and subcommittee assignments (Clerk of the House site). Roll calls: 102nd-107th from Voteview; 101st from ICPSR. Units: Representatives (two-mode nodes) and committees/subcommittees (called "committees"). Detailed example is the 107th House (2001-2002): 444 Representatives including midterm replacements (432 used in the SVD ranking; 443 in the Poole-Rosenthal comparison), 990 roll-call votes (749 used in the Optimal Classification comparison after removing votes with under 0.5% minority), and 113 committees (19 standing plus subcommittees and select committees). The 108th Congress is mentioned only as "data not shown" (Homeland Security grew to 50 members). Intelligence committee has 20 members.
extraction.method: 1) Build a two-mode Representative-by-committee assignment network. 2) Project onto a one-mode committee network; edge weight = "normalized interlock" = observed common members / expected common members if same-size committees were assigned independently at random from the House. Value 1 = chance, 2 = twice chance, 0 = no overlap. 3) Single-linkage hierarchical clustering on normalized interlocks; dendrogram (Fig. 2) read as levels. 4) Visualization by a variant of Kamada-Kawai spring embedding that uses link strengths (Fig. 1). 5) Voting matrix B (n Representatives x m votes; +1 yea, -1 nay, 0 absent/abstain); SVD gives leading eigenvectors u(k), v(k) and singular values; a rank-2 approximation (Eq. 3) is used. Partisan coordinate = eigenvector that tracks party; bipartisan = eigenvector that groups nearly everyone. 6) Extremism e_i = |p_i - mean p| on the partisan coordinate; committee extremism = mean over members; clusters averaged likewise. 7) Vote-outcome reconstruction: sum the rank-2 approximated votes per vote; positive = pass. 8) Compare individual-vote classification with Poole-Rosenthal Optimal Classification (107th only).
extraction.identification: None. The design is descriptive. The random-assignment baseline in normalized interlock is the only null model; no significance test or randomization distribution is reported for any interlock value, extremism ranking, or SVD component. The conclusion that committees are "stacked" rests on departures from that baseline, not on an estimated test.
extraction.scope: Population: all House members and committee assignments in the 101st-108th Congresses (1989-2004); detailed illustration uses the 107th House only. Institution: U.S. House; Senate, party leadership decisions and assignment rules are not modeled. Era: 1989-2004. Partisan control: Democrats 101st-103rd; Republicans 104th-108th (Table 1 lists leadership).

summary_md:
Porter, Mucha, Newman and Warmbrand (PNAS 2005) build a two-mode network of House members and committees for the 101st-108th Congresses and project it onto committee pairs. Each edge is weighted by a "normalized interlock": the number of shared members divided by the number expected if committees of those sizes were filled at random. Single-linkage clustering then finds about four levels of structure: subcommittees, committees, groups of committees, and the whole House. Subcommittees of the same parent form tight cliques; the Intelligence cluster has interlocks of 14.4-26.6 times chance. A separate rank-2 SVD of the 107th House roll-call matrix (990 votes) splits into a bipartisan axis (45.3% of the sum of squares) and a partisan axis (29.6%). It reproduces 92.7% of individual votes, close to Poole-Rosenthal's Optimal Classification at 92.8%. Committees differ in partisan extremism: Rules is 2nd of the 19 standing committees, Select Homeland Security is 4th of all 113, and Intelligence and its subcommittees are among the 10 least extreme. The analysis is descriptive. No interlock, cluster or the "not random" conclusion has a significance test.

The paper bears on the built system in three places. (1) The committee pillar adds every subcommittee seat on top of the parent seat at one-sixth weight, and Porter shows subcommittee membership largely sits inside the parent committee's membership. (2) In the say-do gate, one recorded Yea on a final-passage vote can corroborate a Champion cell, yet the dominant structure in a roll-call matrix is near-unanimous bipartisan agreement. (3) Two components cite Porter for "community structure", but no code uses committee co-membership or a community partition. Melange has no committee co-membership layer; committees enter only as a scalar pillar. Porter's normalized interlock reweights each edge by size. That must not be carried over to cosponsor edges, because per-edge normalization of cosponsor edges was measured and REJECTED.

paul_entries.text:
Mason, Porter, and Peter Mucha. A Network Analysis of Committees in the U.S. House of Representatives | *PNAS*, 5 Apr. 2005, [www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0500191102](http://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0500191102).

This article, conducted by Professors Mason Porter, Peter Mucha, M.E. Newman, and Casey Warmbrand, examines the United States House of Representatives, and more specifically its subcommittees, through the lens of Social Network Analysis, revealing strong linkages within certain committees and a general hierarchical structure. The network consists of two nodes: a two-mode committee network and a one-mode representative network, with edges representing the common overlap between the two. The multi-layering of this social network is prevalent to the current research by directly outlining the entire ecosystem of the U.S House of Representatives on the committee level, and details of the correlations between the overall partisan alignment and committee selection. The main weaknesses are as follows: First for correlation between partisan alignment and committee selection, what came first, the chicken or the egg? Second, which pertains to the present research, is how to display both the members and the committees on the same graph and whether that can be done and/or is feasible.

It holds 45.3% of the sum of squares, against 29.6% for the partisan coordinate. Always guessing 'pass' is right on 735 of 990 votes (74.2%). The Optimal Classification comparison keeps 749 of 990 roll calls after dropping votes with a small minority share; the threshold glyph is lost in extraction.

summary_issues: Says Rules is 2nd of the 19 standing committees. The paper says second most extreme (after Judiciary). Clarify the direction.
Says subcommittee membership largely sits inside the parent committee. The paper gives one example (Intelligence, each subcommittee at least half of the parent) for one Congress.

Says two components cite Porter for community structure. In the repo the template cites Sotoudeh-Porter-Krishnagopal at line 738 and no Porter 2005 or Porter-Mucha-Newman string exists in fec/. The component-record wording was not located, so this stays unverified.
Describes Porter's SVD as a NOMINATE-class method (rel flags). Porter uses an unnormalized SVD benchmarked against Optimal Classification; it is not DW-NOMINATE. Reword.
Says the say-do vote evidence is final-passage. The producer aggregates all Yea or Nay member votes on HS117-119 roll calls linked to bills, with no final-passage filter seen. Clarify.

Says Paul's component position cites Porter as grounding the cosponsor graph. Paul's annotation entries link Porter only to a committee or multi-layer committee network (inferred). Unsupported as stated.

Cites a staffer artifact with r = 0.87 and a 70.8 percent admin-container share. The 70.8 percent appears in employment_history.py line 83; the r = 0.87 figure is not in the repo. Mark as artifact-sourced.
Says Melange has no committee co-membership layer. Verified: none found in fec/network or fec/engine; committees enter only through committee_scores.py.
Paul's paraphrase (two-mode committee network plus one-mode representative network) is a misreading: the paper projects only committees. Verified against lines 76-79.
Paper says no significance test or randomization null for any value; the summary's 'the conclusion is not random' is descriptive and should carry that label.
gaps_exposed: The system has no committee co-membership (two-mode member x committee) layer. Committees reach the engines only as a scalar pillar, so the hierarchy and cross-committee interlocks Porter documents never enter cascades or path-finding.

The roll-call vote evidence (vote_category_lean.json) has no contestedness or minority-share filter. Porter and Poole-Rosenthal show that near-unanimous votes dominate the roll-call matrix and should be screened out before votes are used to tell members apart (OC drops votes with under 0.5% minority).
The committee pillar ignores partisan composition and stacking, and treats subcommittee seats as additive even though Porter shows they nest within the parent.

Nothing in the system builds a member ideal-point or partisan/bipartisan coordinate from roll calls. Porter's SVD gets 92.7% individual-vote reproduction from two coordinates, which would be a cheap baseline for checking whether stance labels add anything beyond party or ideology on CU votes.
There is no random-assignment null for any co-membership edge (committee, caucus or staffer container) against which to judge whether a tie is above chance.
flags: Porter's normalized interlock (observed/expected shared members) is a per-edge size normalization. Per-edge normalization was measured and REJECTED for the cosponsor network (brain topics/2026-06-feature-cosponsor-and-sector-networks.md:101). Do not recommend porting it to cosponsor edges; at most it belongs on a new committee layer, UNVERIFIED.

Porter's SVD roll-call coordinates are a NOMINATE-class ideal-point method. Paul rejected DW-NOMINATE vote edges for the signed coalitions (same brain note, line 93). Do not re-propose SVD-derived vote edges.

Citation drift: melange-pathfinding.multi-target-and-budget-modes and melange-sna.cosponsor-network cite Porter et al. 2005 for community structure in a cosponsor graph, but the paper analyzes committee co-membership and the built code has no community partition. The Porter-lineage paper on cosponsorship is Sotoudeh-Porter-Krishnagopal 2024.

Committee 'extremism' and 'stacking' in Porter are descriptive, with no significance test or randomization null. Any wording that committees 'are stacked' should carry that label and its window (107th House, 113 committees).

The say-do bearing is a candidate check, not a measured defect. The share of lopsided votes behind Path V corroborations has not been computed; it stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
paul_alignment: Paul's takeaways broadly match the paper (strong within-committee ties, a general hierarchy, and partisan alignment correlating with committee selection), with one misreading. He describes "a two-mode committee network and a one-mode representative network", but the paper projects the two-mode network onto a committee-to-committee network; representatives are not projected. His Weakness 1 (chicken-or-egg causality) is correct and stronger than he states: the paper has no identification and no significance test at all. His Weakness 2 (can members and committees share one graph?) is answered by the paper itself, since the two-mode assignment network is exactly that graph. His inferred system link, "multi-layer committee network for the present research", is stale against the built system. Melange has no committee co-membership layer; committees enter only as the Influence pillar scalar (committee_scores.py), and the components that cite Porter for community structure do not implement any. His committee-pillar position that "committees are the structural layer of the House" holds, but as built the pillar uses neither the interlock structure nor partisan composition.

extraction.coverage: Read the full text file (33,059 lines) in chunks: main text PDF pp.1-42 including references, and supplemental materials from about PDF p.43 to the end, including the supplement's reference list. Figure and table glyph lines (axis ticks, single-letter legend codes, state abbreviations) were filtered out with awk; every figure caption and every word-bearing table was read. All 93 annotation items were read. Page numbers are PDF pages, matching the annotation numbering; printed page = PDF page minus 1. Supplement PDF pages are approximate unless anchored by an annotation.
extraction.research_question: How can ideal points be estimated for candidates and contributors across federal and state elections, for incumbents and non-incumbents, from campaign contribution records? Secondary: whether ideology or strategic motives (investor, partisan-electoral) drive contributions, and whether the resulting common-space CFscores are valid and stable enough for work on polarization, state politics, candidate positioning and donor ideology.
extraction.theory: Spatial model of giving (PDF pp.6-7, Eq. 1): contributor i allocates amounts y_j across recipients to maximize sum of b_i(y_j) - c_i(y_j) - y_j(delta_j - theta_i)^2, subject to y_j below the legal limit clim_j. Competing accounts tested: the investor model (contributions as payments for access or votes; Denzau and Munger 1986, Snyder 1990), the partisan electoral model (donors fund competitive races to shift party seat share; Wand 2007, 2012), and the ideological model (proximity only). Central claim: individual donors give mainly on ideology, so spatial giving is the appropriate model for individuals and most PACs (PDF pp.22-23).
extraction.data: Campaign finance records: over 103 million records, 1979-2012, from 13.4 million individuals and 511,141 organizations to 51,572 candidates and 6,408 committees (PDF p.9; abstract says "over 100 million"). Scaling sample (PDF p.10): 3.93 million individuals plus 261,828 committees and organizations as contributor rows; 13,189 federal candidates, 55,737 state candidates and 9,436 committees as recipient columns. An additional 9.75 million single-recipient donors are projected onto the space as supplementary observations. Inclusion: contributor gave to at least 2 recipients; candidate received from at least 2 contributors; loans and transfers excluded; individual gifts to labor, corporate and trade PACs excluded; corporate and trade PACs excluded from estimation. Unit: contributor-recipient pair; amounts converted to counts of $100 bins capped at 50 ($5,000+). Strategic-giving tests: 5,000 random individuals with at least 25 federal contributions 2004-2012 (N=49,418 for the full 25+ group in the consistency test), 124 labor PACs, 1,312 corporate and trade PACs (PDF pp.18-19). Roll-call comparisons: 96th-112th Congresses. Period-specific estimates require at least 25 contributors per candidate per cycle.
extraction.method: Augmented correspondence analysis (CA) on the contributor-by-recipient contingency matrix R (PDF p.7; supplement). Matrix is standardized and decomposed by SVD of K = D_r^(-1/2)(R - rc')D_c^(-1/2); contributor ideal points theta = U D^-1/2 scaled, recipient delta = V D^-1/2. CA is described as nearly equivalent to a log-linear ideal point model (Lowe 2008; ter Braak 1985). Steps: (1) scale federal elections first; (2) scale each state separately, using bridge contributors (those giving to both state and federal races), with an 8-step alternating least-squares routine; (3) jointly re-estimate recipients; (4) normalize so the weighted mean and SD of contribution amounts are 0 and 1. Between-set identification: contributor points are regressed on matched candidate points with an error-in-variables specification (intercept 0.017, slope 0.975, on 29,913 candidates who appear as donors). Presidential nominees get separate pre- and post-nomination scores. Non-incumbent scores: contributor points held fixed; candidate points re-estimated from pre-record contributions. Period-specific CFscores follow Nokken and Poole (2004). Strategic-giving comparison: a right-censored negative binomial count model per donor (IRT-style, adapted from Bonica 2013a), compared by log-likelihood and the Cameron-Windmeijer deviance residual RDev.
extraction.identification: Bridging through multi-office donors, not roll calls. 70-90% of contributors who fund state campaigns also give to federal campaigns (PDF p.8), and candidates running for both state and federal office add more bridges. The federal scaling anchors each state's scaling. A final rescaling aligns contributor and candidate distances. Identification is up to a standard normalization. The author argues that the cross-state identification assumption is "unheroic and verifiable": donors have the same ideal point when giving to state and federal candidates (PDF p.24 footnote 13; state-federal correlation 0.88 for all donors, 0.93 for donors to 10+ candidates).
extraction.scope: US campaigns, 1979-2012. Candidates for President, Congress, governors, state attorneys general, secretaries of state, other state-wide offices, state legislatures, state supreme courts, federal circuit courts, boards of education and ballot campaigns (PDF p.23, Fig. 2). Also donors, labor, corporate and trade PACs and industry aggregates. Institutions: federal and all 50 states. Claims are about ideology as revealed by giving; no claim about legislative behavior is tested beyond roll-call comparisons.

limitations: Author states that CFscores are not the 'true' ideology measure, that roll-call and contribution measures are expected to differ, and that perfect correspondence is neither expected nor desirable (PDF p.12).
Strategic giving may bias estimates. The author reports covariate effects at the margins and argues the bias is small, but does not rule it out (PDF pp.21-22; supplement).

Party-driven classification: CFscores classify moderates who overlap the opposing party poorly; the classification gap to DW-NOMINATE narrows for close votes but not lopsided votes (supplement, 'Roll Call Classification, cont.').

Contribution Accounting Assumption: CA cannot control non-spatial covariates such as incumbency or committee assignments; the IRT count model can, but it is computationally infeasible at full scale (PDF pp.7-8).

Cross-state bridging depends on the assumption that donors hold the same ideal point when giving to state and federal candidates; the author calls it 'unheroic and verifiable' but does not test it directly beyond the 0.88 and 0.93 correlations (PDF p.24 fn 13).

Record linkage errors. Corporate board members were the training set: 57% were assigned a single ID; 42% were split (type 1, information loss); 13% failed the 90% threshold. Two type-2 errors merged different people (family members at the same employer), and type 2 errors can bias estimates (supplement, Record Linkage; PDF p.51). Disclosure of address and occupation is weaker in the 1980s and early 1990s.

Sample restrictions drive results: individual gifts to labor, corporate and trade PACs are dropped; corporate and trade PACs are excluded from estimation because of mixed motives; candidates need 2+ contributors and contributors need 2+ recipients; period-specific scores need 25+ contributors per cycle (PDF pp.9-10, 15).
Assumption: fixed legislator ideal points in the polarization trends exclude ideological adaptation, so the trends capture replacement but not adaptation (PDF p.30 fn 15).
Presidential nominees: joint fundraising after nomination shifts estimates, so the author uses pre-nomination scores as more accurate (supplement; PDF p.47).
Pro-life share interpretation is ambiguous: the author says it could reflect economic dimension dominance or the limits of stated positions (PDF pp.32-33).

summary_md:
Bonica (SSRN draft, 2013) estimates common-space ideal points (CFscores) for candidates and donors. The data are more than 100 million federal and state contribution records from 1979 to 2012, and the method is correspondence analysis on a contributor-by-recipient matrix. Donors who give in both state and federal races bridge the two levels. Pooled across parties, candidate CFscores track DW-NOMINATE at r = 0.92 (unstratified). Within party the correlation is much weaker: 0.56 to 0.72. Scores for non-incumbents predict their later roll-call scores about as well as incumbent scores do.

For this system, the important result is the test of why people give. On 5,000 individual donors with 25 or more federal gifts (2004-2012), the ideological model beats both the partisan electoral model and the investor model by log-likelihood. The investor model barely beats the baseline. For corporate and trade PACs the investor model is competitive, and in its unconstrained form it fits better than the ideological model (Table 2). That is why those PACs are left out of estimation.

Three consequences follow:
1. The paper does not show that dollars buy more in competitive seats. The partisan electoral model, which Paul highlighted, loses to the ideological model for individual donors.
2. CU and bank PAC money is exactly the mixed-motive class. Because individual donors give by ideology, money and stance are entangled, so any test of whether money moves members needs an ideology control.
3. The record-linkage appendix gives Mentat's identity ladder a concrete error profile. When merges went wrong, they joined family members at the same employer.

The paper measures who gives and why. It does not test whether giving changes votes or buys access, so it cannot calibrate any money-response constant.

extraction.title: Influencing Connected Legislators
extraction.venue: NBER Working Paper No. 22739 (October 2016; JEL D72, D78). Not peer-reviewed per the NBER disclaimer. Metadata hint confirmed: authors, year, and NBER w22739 are correct.
extraction.document_type: NBER working paper (theory plus empirical estimation)
extraction.coverage: Read all 3,019 lines of the text file (110,304 chars, under the 400,000 limit) in six chunks. Covered: front matter, abstract, Introduction (Sec 1), Model (Sec 2), Equilibrium contributions (Sec 3 incl. Lemma 1, Props 1-3), Evidence from the U.S. Congress (Sec 4 incl. data, controls, networks, Heckman/control-function correction, results), Discussion and extensions (Sec 5), Conclusions (Sec 6), References, Appendix proofs (Sec 7), and Tables 1-5 with notes. Not in the text file: Tables A.1-A.3 (data appendix), the online appendix (Lemma 3.1/3.2 proofs, Lemma 1 policy-motivated proof, Sec 5 threshold derivations), and any figure beyond the textual description of Figure 1. Paul's markup: no markup files were listed for this PDF (task specified none), so paul_markup is empty.
extraction.research_question: Do legislators' social ties affect how interest groups allocate campaign contributions? Specifically, how do interest groups allocate money across legislators connected by a social network, and do legislators' network positions (Bonacich centrality) predict PAC contributions in the U.S. House?
extraction.theory: Two interest groups (one for policy A, one against) each have a budget and promise contingent payments to legislators, who vote after observing offers. Legislators value contributions (concave utility, log in the estimation), value conformity with their social network (weights G, so utility rises with peers voting the same way), and may care about the policy (policy motivation; office-motivated legislators have zero policy preference). Interest groups do not know legislators' preferences exactly (uniform noise with density Psi). Under Assumptions 1 (sufficient noise, Psi small) and 2 (I - beta*G invertible and positive), there is a unique pure-strategy Nash equilibrium (Props 1-2). With office-motivated legislators the equilibrium transfers maximize a weighted sum of legislators' monetary utilities with weights equal to Bonacich centralities (Prop 1, Sec 3.2.1). With policy-motivated legislators the weights are modified Bonacich centralities (eq. 15, Prop 2). As the number of legislators grows, or as policy preference weakens, the modified weights converge to simple Bonacich centralities (Corollary 1; Prop 3, Sec 3.2.2). The central empirical implication is that the network externality parameter (phi*) must be positive for social ties to matter.
extraction.data: Unit: legislator-Congress observations for U.S. House members (stacked across Congresses). Sample periods: 109th-113th Congresses (election cycles 2004-2012). Each committee network has roughly 440 Representatives (including midterm replacements) and about 20 standing committees; the alumni network has over 400 nodes and thousands of links (fn. 11). Regression N: committee-network specification 2,128 observations; alumni-network specification 1,166 observations (more than 50% of congressmen linked by alma mater; Sec 4.2.1). Dependent variable: total PAC contributions to each candidate in $ millions, from FEC files aggregated by the Center for Responsive Politics, trimmed at 1st and 99th percentiles; range $9,519 to $7,178,406; total PAC spending $310 million (110th) to $453 million (112th) (Sec 4.2.2). Cosponsorship data for Table 1: all bills proposed in the House 109th-113th Congresses from THOMAS (244,519 dyads for alumni-cosponsorship; 242,735 dyads for committee-membership). Controls: margin of victory (FEC publications, supplemented by state agencies), per capita income by district (ACS one-year estimates), DW-NOMINATE first dimension (Nokken-Poole modified coordinates), committee chair, seniority, relevant powerful committee (Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Appropriations, Rules, Financial Services), joint committee (Economic, Taxation, Library, Printing), party (Republican=1), gender, top-10 university attendance (about 6% of congressmen), four election-cycle dummies. Committee and roster data: Clerk of the House, Stewart and Woon site, CQ roster for the 113th; alumni: Biographical Directory of Congress; ideology/party/gender: GovTrack.
extraction.method: Theory: backward induction over a two-stage game (voting stage then influence stage); existence by Brouwer; uniqueness via Lemma 1 (unique voting equilibrium when office-motivated, or policy-motivated with sufficient uncertainty); equilibrium characterized as maximization of weighted monetary utilities (Props 1-2). Empirical: a spatial autoregressive (SAR) model, s = alpha*1 + phi* W s + beta'X + eps (eq. 23), where s is log-transformed contribution-related outcome (eq. 17-18 derive log utility FOC; eq. 20-22 derive the SAR form), estimated by maximum likelihood (Anselin 1988). Benchmarks: OLS without network effects, AIC comparisons, likelihood-ratio test of phi*=0 (chi-square, 1 df), and OLS with degree, betweenness and closeness centrality (Table 4). Robustness: party-weighted committee network, chairmanship-weighted committee network, alumni networks with graduation-period windows (4 and 2 years). Multiple interest groups (Sec 5.2), threshold objectives (Sec 5.3) and heterogeneous policies (Sec 5.4) are extensions that leave the SAR form unchanged up to scale.
extraction.identification: Committee network: links are proportional to shared committees, which may be endogenous to unobserved legislator traits that also drive contributions. The authors use a control-function (Heckman-style) correction following Qu and Lee (2015): a first-stage linear probability dyadic model of committee sharing on characteristic distances (eq. 24), then the first-stage residual term is added to the outcome equation (eq. 25). Exclusion: dyad-specific variables in link formation are excluded from the outcome equation; Table 2 column (2) reports the correction. The assumption that the selection effect is the same for all politicians is stated in fn. 23. Alumni network: asserted exogenous by construction to the political process, since shared institutions predate election; no selection correction is applied. Validity of the alumni network is argued via Table 1 panel (a) (alumni links predict cosponsorship) and panel (b) (alumni links barely predict committee sharing, R^2 0.002-0.003). Cosponsorship is not used to build the network because it is endogenous to contributions (fn. 30).
extraction.scope: Population: U.S. House of Representatives members serving in the 109th through 113th Congresses (election cycles 2004-2012), with PAC contributions from FEC/CRP data. Institution: Congress with House committee structure and PAC campaign finance. Era: 2004-2012 cycles. Theory applies to any network with a finite number of legislator types. The authors note that the theory is about monetary transfers and social networks in legislatures generally. Not studied: Senate, state legislatures, non-monetary resources, lobbyist behavior, and endogenous changes in network topology.

key_findings.finding: Equilibrium exists and is unique in pure strategies under Assumption 1 (noise sufficiently large) and Assumption 2; with office-motivated legislators the optimal transfer allocation maximizes a weighted sum of monetary utilities with weights equal to Bonacich centralities. Under log utility the transfer is proportional to Bonacich centrality.
key_findings.numbers: Assumption 1: Psi*(beta_max + ...) <= 1/2 (bound on the noise density Psi); Assumption 2: I - 2*Psi*G invertible and positive. Proportionality factor depends on the shadow cost of money.

key_findings.finding: With policy-motivated legislators the allocation weights become modified Bonacich centralities that depend on preferences and pivot probabilities; they converge to simple Bonacich centralities as the policy-preference weight goes to zero and as the number of legislators grows large.
key_findings.location: Sec 3.2.2 (eq. 15-16, Prop 2, p. 15); Corollary 1 (p. 15-16); Prop 3 (p. 16); proof in Sec 7.3 (p. 39-40)
key_findings.numbers: Prop 3: convergence as n goes to infinity; the proof uses Lemma 3.2 (pivot probabilities and their derivatives go to zero).

key_findings.finding: Committee-network estimate of the network externality parameter is positive and significant; with the control-function correction it is slightly larger.
Alumni-network estimate of the externality parameter is positive and significant.
Network effects significantly improve model fit over OLS without network terms; the likelihood ratio test rejects phi = 0 in both networks.
key_findings.numbers: Committee: AIC OLS 5686.323 vs MLE 5679.196; LR statistic 11.127. Alumni: AIC OLS 3201.537 vs MLE 3193.922; LR statistic 9.615. Table brackets show p = 0.003 (committee) and p = 0.001 (alumni), while the text says p-value equal to 0.000.

key_findings.finding: Standard centrality measures (degree, closeness, betweenness) do not explain PAC contributions; the model with them fits no better than the no-network baseline.
key_findings.numbers: Degree 0.0004 (SE 0.0003) in committee network, -0.0018 (SE 0.0053) in alumni network; Closeness 0.5902 (SE 0.4711) and 0.5903 (SE 0.4771); Betweenness -4.9e-05* (SE 2.9e-05) in committee network, -3.2e-05 (SE 5e-05) in alumni; R^2 = 0.148 across all Table 4 specifications.

key_findings.finding: Results are robust to party-weighted and chairmanship-weighted committee networks and to alumni networks restricted to overlapping graduation periods. The party-weighted estimate is larger than baseline.
key_findings.numbers: Party-weighted committee network: phi = 0.2486*** (SE 0.0656) MLE; 0.2588*** corrected. Chairmanship-weighted: 0.3575*** (SE 0.0866) and 0.2152*** (corrected). Alumni, 4-year window: 0.07700*** (SE 0.0290), N = 767. Alumni, 2-year window: 0.06694** (SE 0.0306), N = 597.

key_findings.finding: Alumni links strongly predict cosponsorship but barely predict committee sharing, supporting the claim that the alumni network is a distinct channel from committee-based ties.
key_findings.numbers: Alumni link on cosponsorship: 0.180*** (SE 0.008) bare, 0.069*** (SE 0.007) with controls; R^2 rises from 0.008 to 0.11. Alumni link on committee membership: 0.006 (SE 0.006) bare, 0.012* (SE 0.007) with controls; R^2 0.002-0.003. Authors state the alumni network explains less than 1% of committee formation versus about 11% of endorsement.

key_findings.finding: Control coefficients have the signs the literature predicts: chairs and relevant-committee members get more PAC money; close races, ideological extremity and seniority are associated with lower or higher contributions as stated; Republicans receive more.
key_findings.numbers: Chair 0.4006*** (SE 0.0967) committee; Margin of Victory -0.8972*** (SE 0.0885); DW_ideology -1.0774*** (SE 0.1241); Party (Republican) 0.1443** (SE 0.0573); Per capita income 0.0061** (SE 0.0025).

limitations: Authors describe this as a first attempt to bring predictions to data; they note significant room for further analysis (Sec 6, p. 30-31).
Theory covers only monetary transfers; non-monetary resources (expertise, contacts) are left for future work (Sec 6).
Interest groups do not alter network topology in the model; linking that to Ballester, Calvo-Armengol and Zenou (2006) key-player analysis is left open (Sec 6).

Committee network may be endogenous; the control-function correction is parametric and assumes the selection effect is identical across legislators (fn. 23); the selection term's sign suggests unobserved expertise drives both contributions and network links (Sec 4.3).
Bootstrapped standard errors (1,000 replications) are used because no closed-form adjustment exists for the generated regressor (fn. 25).
Alumni sample (N = 1,166) oversamples top-10 university graduates; a top-10 dummy is included, and top-10 attendance is about 6% of congressmen (Sec 4.2.2).
Cosponsorship is not used as the network because it is itself an endogenous outcome (fn. 30).
Policy-motivated case requires sufficient uncertainty (Assumption 3 / Lemma 1); the proofs for policy-motivated legislators are in the online appendix, not the text file.
Modified Bonacich weights are laborious to compute for large networks and depend on preferences and the voting rule, not only topology (Sec 3.2.2, p. 15).
Closed-form Bonacich relation depends on utility specification (fn. 3); logarithmic utility is assumed for the empirical mapping (Sec 4.1).

Reviewer-level caveats from this extraction: the text layer garbles Greek symbols (phi*, beta, psi, Psi), so the exact formula defining the SAR parameter is reconstructed from surrounding text. The text states p = 0.000 for the LR tests but the table brackets show 0.003 and 0.001. The introduction says the outcome is business PAC contributions, while Sec 4.2.2 describes total PAC contributions. Table A.1 (variable definitions and summary statistics) is not in the text file.
measures: Bonacich centrality b(beta,G) = (I - beta*G)^{-1} * 1 (eq. 4), with decay parameter beta; modified Bonacich (eq. 15).
Dependent variable: total PAC contributions to each congressman, $ millions (trimmed at 1st/99th percentiles).
Committee network link: number of shared committees (count), with party-weighted and chairmanship-weighted variants.
Alumni network link: 1 if two members graduated from the same institution (undergraduate or graduate); variants require overlapping graduation periods of 4 or 2 years.
Degree centrality (count of direct links), betweenness centrality, closeness centrality (normalized by degree).

Control variables: margin of victory, per capita district income, DW-NOMINATE dimension 1, chair, seniority, relevant committee, joint committee, party, gender, top-10 university, election-cycle dummies.
Cosponsorship link counts (directional) from THOMAS for Table 1.
Fit measures: AIC, likelihood-ratio statistic (chi-square, 1 df), R^2 for OLS benchmarks.

summary_md:
Battaglini and Patacchini model two opposed interest groups that bid for votes from legislators who care about money and about voting the same way as their peers. They prove the game has a unique equilibrium. When legislators are office-motivated and have log utility, each group pays each legislator in proportion to that legislator's Bonacich (Katz-Bonacich) centrality. When legislators also care about policy, the weights become a modified Bonacich centrality that depends on preferences and pivot probabilities, and it converges back to plain Bonacich in large chambers. The empirical part fits a spatial-autoregressive model of total PAC money to U.S. House members across the 2004-2012 cycles. Ties come from shared committees (N=2,128 member-Congress rows, phi=0.209, 0.217 after a control-function correction) and shared alma maters (N=1,166, phi=0.084). Degree, closeness and betweenness explain nothing: R^2 stays at 0.148, the same as the model with no network terms. The authors chose not to build the network from cosponsorship, because cosponsorship is itself driven by money (fn. 30). This is an NBER working paper and has not been peer-reviewed.

The most direct bearing is on `fec/engine/kb_benchmark.py`, which cites this paper and implements its prediction as a diagnostic. Its design departs from the paper in three ways:
- It runs Katz on the cosponsorship-based kernel `build_P`, the network the paper avoids because cosponsorship depends on money.
- It pools the Senate with the House, while the paper covers the House only.
- It sets attenuation at 0.85 of the convergence bound, where the paper estimates a weaker spillover of about 0.08 to 0.25.

The stored results (Spearman rho 0.135 against CU money and 0.230 against bank plus financial-services money, n=533 across both chambers, file written 2026-08-18) are therefore unstratified, unverified, and about seven weeks stale. The paper also offers modest support, on a money outcome only, for keeping the degree/betweenness InfluenceScore out of the rank. It also points to a gap: in the allocator, money to one member reaches that member's network neighbours only after a discrete conversion.

bearings.paper_claim: Office-motivated legislators with log utility get transfers exactly proportional to their Bonacich centrality b = (I - beta*G)^-1 * 1 (Prop 1, eq 4, eq 17-18). With policy-motivated legislators the weights become modified Bonacich centralities depending on preferences and pivot probabilities (eq 15, Prop 2), which converge to the office-motivated allocation as the number of legislators grows (Prop 3). Reported network externality phi = 0.2088 (SE 0.0697) committee, 0.2165 (SE 0.0703) corrected, 0.0837 (SE 0.0262) alumni (Table 2).

bearings.system_side: kb_benchmark.py computes KB centrality on build_P(load_network()) with an out-walk matvec and delta = KB_DELTA (0.85) / spectral radius; stored radius 1.5019 and delta 0.56595 match. Docstring lines 2-5 say groups allocate IN PROPORTION TO KB centrality. The member desk reads kb_pct from the stored file.

The KB attenuation (KB_DELTA 0.85 in kb_benchmark.py; attenuation_fraction 0.82 in the dashboard template) is set near the convergence bound, not estimated. Nothing estimates a network-externality parameter with a likelihood-ratio test against a no-network baseline, as the paper's SAR maximum-likelihood fit does.

The benchmark is raw Spearman with no controls. The paper shows margin of victory, DW-NOMINATE, chair, party and seniority are large predictors of PAC money, so an uncontrolled rho mixes centrality with these covariates.
kb_benchmark pools both chambers and is not stratified by chamber or party. The paper's evidence is House-only.
In the joint optimizer, money spills over to peers only through discrete conversions, with no continuous network multiplier on the value of a dollar.
